newsitem.title: ISRAEL: PLO police between a rock and a hard place.
newsitem.headline: PLO police between a rock and a hard place.

text.p: Ayman did not seem to notice the blood running down his leg. He was struggling to keep hold of the slingshot that a Palestinian policeman was trying to wrench from his hand.
Across the street another Palestinian policeman whirred a sling over his head and sent a rock across the Hebron rooftops towards Israeli soldiers picking off protesters with rubber bullets.

The David and Goliath battle raging in the West Bank town on Wednesday pointed up the dilemma faced by Yasser Arafat's police force and shed light on the tactics the Palestinian president has adopted on the political battlefield with Israel.
Ayman was among the hundreds of youths who flowed through porous police lines after a "martyr's" funeral to take on Israeli soldiers in full battle gear with rocks and occasional petrol bombs.
He hopped up a side alley after an Israeli rubber bullet bounced into his shin. But he still managed to let off a few stones at soldiers crouched under a shop front.
"Leave me alone" the youngster yelled. "We have to fight."
The policeman relented. Ayman pocketed his slingshot and slumped in a doorway, at last aware of the pain in his leg.
The policeman, who declined to speak, merely shrugged his shoulders and smiled. A few officers dragged stone-throwers out of range of the Israelis but the youths quickly regrouped.

Back in the main street, demonstrators pointed in delight at a group of policemen on a roof. One was getting increasingly accurate with his sling. When his colleagues noticed a press photographer they stopped him.

After about an hour when initial passions had cooled, the police, unarmed in this part of Hebron under a peace deal with Israel, move in with jeeps to push the crowd back from the borders of the Jewish settler enclaves which have become the flashpoint for violence in this partitioned city.

"The Palestinian police are caught in a dilemma," said one PLO official, who asked not to be identified. "They are obliged to prevent clashes but they are afraid that if they do not let protesters show their anger their own people will turn on them."

Arafat's myriad security services, which have ballooned from an originally-envisioned 9,000 to more than 20,000, gained popularity among activists after they fired back at Israeli soldiers last year during stone-throwing protests that quickly turned into gunbattles. Fifty-one Palestinians and 15 Israeli soldiers died.

In a poll published on Wednesday 37.5 percent of Palestinians said the police should not stop street battles with Israelis. In fact, 31.3 percent said the police should encourage protests, according to the survey by the Jerusalem Media and Communications Centre.
Israelis charge that Arafat could snuff out the street battles and curb Islamic suicide bombers if he chose.
They believe he is trying to use the violence to reinforce a weak political hand in bargaining with Israel's Benjamin Netanyahu.

"Arafat and the Palestinian Authority are for perhaps the first time using the violence and terrorism as a means to achieve their political aims," the head of Israeli army intelligence, Major-General Moshe Yaalon, said on Wednesday.

Israeli security sources claim that Arafat has not attacked the infrastructure of "terrorist" groups. They say he selectively allows street protests to flare for several hours before sending in his police.

"This is not true," said Jibril Rajoub, overall PLO security chief for the West Bank. He denied Arafat was turning the tap of violence off and on to send a message to Netanyahu and his U.S. allies that the PLO chairman could not be ignored.

"We don't do it to send a message through bloodshed," Rajoub told Reuters, blaming Israeli settlement policy for the violence. "People express their denunciation and anger in a demonstration and it is our responsibility to try to prevent any friction with the Israelis in the adjacent areas."
"We are here to convince people," he said of the stone-throwers. "Sometimes we fail, sometimes we succeed."
Ayman was not convinced. He still had his sling and said despite his leg he'd be back tomorrow.
